lines.note: Closes the preceding page's gloss with 'with the community'; this is a continuation, not a new Japanese entry.

Fazzuxi / fa zzu ſu is hazushi/hazusu, detaching or removing. On enlarged second inspection the unusual printed ending is retained as uita, also recorded by NINJAL; it should not be silently regularized to the expected conjugation.

runs.text: couſa doutra: ajuntaſe eſte verbo às raizes de

lines.note: The Portuguese explains separation of one thing from another and says this verb combines with other verbal stems.
Moushi-hazusu illustrates speaking amiss or failing to say the intended thing; Errar begins the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: no falar, ou deixar de falar o que queria eſque-

lines.note: The gloss describes forgetting to say what one wanted. Deixar restores the missing consonant in OCR dei ar; the sentence continues through esquecendo-lhe.
Mihazusu is to overlook or fail to see. The opening fragment completes the preceding explanation of forgetting.
The failure to see is through error or inattention. The next example begins kutsuwa, abumi: bit and stirrups, with abumi split across rows.
Abumi nado wo hazusu means removing stirrups and similar tack. Freo and estribos supply the matching Portuguese objects.
Ao cavalo completes the explanation: remove that equipment from the horse. No Japanese word begins here.
Hazushigane denotes removable metal fittings; the gloss explicitly includes silver, gold, and other metal.

runs.text: que ſe faz deſmanchar, & tira de ſeu lugar

lines.note: These fittings are dismantled and taken out of their place. Desmanchar is the relevant Portuguese verb, not a Japanese continuation.

runs.text: pera ſe gastar como da Catana, &c.

lines.note: The metal can then be spent or used; Catana is an embedded Japanese sword term within the Portuguese explanation, printed in italic here.

runs.text: Aſas que ſeruem aos paſſaros como

lines.note: Hazue is explained through a bird's wings serving as a support. This historical falconry sense should not be replaced by a modern everyday gloss.

runs.text: de bordão quando eſtão canſados, principalmẽte

lines.note: The comparison is to a staff when the birds are tired, especially in the case specified next. The missing c in OCR principalmente was checked against the word.
The entry particularly concerns falcons. Hazue wo tsuku introduces the act of resting on the wings; the initial Portuguese word is se, not le.

runs.text: Deſcanſaro paſſaro ſobre as aſas quã-

lines.note: The opening qu completes tsuku. The gloss describes a bird resting on its wings; the condition continues on the following row.

runs.text: do està canſado, ou com fome. ¶

lines.note: The bird is tired or hungry. A second equivalent Japanese construction begins with the divided hazu-.
Completes hazue ni sugaru, relying on the wings for support; Idem explicitly refers back to the preceding gloss.
He is the bow of a ship, as confirmed by proa do navio. The oversized F belongs to this headword and must remain visible with it.
A separate he entry means a fart or wind. The example he wo continues below; OCR Fz is incompatible with both the visible e and the example.

Firu completes he wo hiru, passing wind. The medial r is very worn and was lost by OCR; its restoration is context-assisted rather than evidence for an otherwise unexplained verb hiu. B marks low usage.
He, uru / feru, eta is the verb 'pass, elapse'. The scan supports initial F, not B, and feru rather than foru; toshi begins the example.
Toshi, tsuki, hi, jidai wo furu lists years, months, days, and ages passing. The Japanese month word exposes OCR tguqi as tçuqi.
The Portuguese completes that time list. Ho wo heru introduces a different application, laying out warp threads.
Estender os fios no tear explains arranging threads on the loom. Hodo wo heru returns to passing a span of time.
Passar algum tempo confirms hodo wo heru. Annai wo heru is the following example, whose historical h-row reading is retained.

runs.text: Dar recado, ou fazer a ſaber a alguem.

lines.note: The annai example is explained as delivering a message or informing somebody, not traversing a physical guide.
Heagari / heagaru is glossed as rising, with rank or dignity specified on the next row. Do not normalize the historical verb from modern expectations.
Em dignidade supplies the figurative field of advancement in rank rather than merely climbing upward.
Hebi is snake; Cobra makes the initial-F correction from OCR B unambiguous linguistically and the scan is compatible.

runs.text: Hũa doença que vem aos meninos como

lines.note: Hebo names a childhood illness compared with measles, not the unrelated modern senses one might associate with hebo.
Sarampao is the measles comparison. X marks regional usage, and Cami introduces the contrasting regional name continued below.
Completes Fe-nano, henano, the Cami equivalent of the preceding disease name. It is not an independent nano entry.
A second hebo entry denotes a creature or insect. The F initial must not become the OCR sequence siebo.

runs.text: Hum certo genero de abobaras como

lines.note: Hechima is a gourd, compared here with cucumbers. Both the following hechima-no example and the visible initial support correction of recnima.
Cogombros completes the cucumber comparison for hechima; preserve this historical Portuguese spelling.
Hechima no kawa is the outer material of the loofah gourd, here described as a covering taken from those cucumber-like fruits.

runs.text: ſe tira pera deſpois com ella raſpar a çugidade

lines.note: The material is removed to scrub dirt away afterward. Se tira and depois restore intelligible Portuguese where OCR lost or confused letters.
Do corpo specifies dirt from the body, confirming the bathing use of the loofah material.
Heko is glossed as an encacho, a covering or loincloth, with B marking low usage. A propria palavra introduces more usual alternatives.
Shitaobi and hada no obi name the undergarment or body sash. The first initial is the printed X of shita-, not OCR A.
Heko wo kaku is putting on that covering. The Portuguese verb is Por; then a second heko sense begins across the break.

runs.text: Hum circulo de cordas. ou canas ſobre

lines.note: The second heko is a circular structure of ropes or canes used for carrying. Circulo is visibly and semantically preferable to cerculo.

runs.text: q̃ poem pedras, & as leuão muitos: ordinaria

lines.note: Stones are placed on it and carried by several people. The initial abbreviation q̃ supplies 'on which'; it is not an isolated capital A.
Completes ordinariamente and gives Ixibeco as the usual name for the stone-carrying apparatus, marked X. Enlarged second inspection supports the looped b; the first-pass f reading was withdrawn.
Hekusokazura is the strongly smelling plant; fede muito explains the name through its smell. Muito corrects OCR murto without changing typography elsewhere.
Hedatari / hedataru means being separated. The gloss begins apartado and the divided word continues below.
Completes dividido: separated and divided. This short Portuguese continuation is part of the same entry.
Hedate is separation or division. The example hed ate wo suru is physically divided after Fe-, not a separate headword below.
Completes hedate wo suru: create separation. Item introduces a further sense of discriminating between people.

runs.text: Fazer diferença de hum, & de outro em fauo-

lines.note: This sense is making a distinction between one person and another in granting favor; favorecer continues across the row boundary.
Completes favorecer and closes the differential-treatment sense of hedate.
Hedate / hedatsuru is the transitive separation verb, glossed as setting apart or distancing.
Hito ni kokoro wo hedatsuru describes emotional distance from someone. Alienado begins the explanation of withdrawn communication.

runs.text: nado ſem ſe communicar com alguem. ¶

lines.note: The gloss says being estranged and not communicating. The next example begins yama, split after Ya-.

runs.text: ma, cuni, vmi, caua, nadouo fedatçuru.

lines.note: Yama, kuni, umi, kawa nado wo hedatsuru lists mountains, countries, sea, and rivers as intervening separations.

runs.text: Estar ſeparado, & diuidido metendoſe no meo

lines.note: The Portuguese explains separation by such things lying between the parties or places, using historical no meo.
Montes, reinos, mar, rios matches the Japanese list of intervening geographical barriers.
Hedo and hedo wo tsuku concern vomiting. The Portuguese infinitive begins Vo and finishes below; lexical joining does not require adding a hyphen.
Completes vomitar and marks the expression B, low usage.
Hehe is glossed with Latin Muliebria, a euphemistic anatomical expression for female genitalia; it is not the OCR nonword Maliebria.
Hege / heguru is becoming detached or unstuck. Despegar-se and desgrudar-se support the restored initial F and the missing Portuguese s.

runs.text: Hũas taboinhas quadradas ſobre que po

lines.note: Hegi denotes small square boards or trays. The following row specifies what is placed on them.
The tray holds a sakazuki with a delicacy. Sacazzuqi is Japanese embedded in Portuguese and should be available for typeface correction.
Hegi / hegu means peeling, opening, or splitting. Enlarging the ending resolves it as eida, heida; this is also NINJAL's indexed paradigm, but the visible e is the transcription evidence.
Ita wo hegu means splitting boards; taboas is divided between this row and the next.

runs.text: boas como fazem às taboinhas com que telhão as

lines.note: The example concerns the thin boards used to roof houses. Telhao derives from telhar, making the missing l consequential.
After casas closes the roofing example, Diminuir introduces reduction; Chigyo begins at the row end.
Chigyo wo hegu is reducing someone's revenue or landholding, matching renda and terras. The printed long-o mark belongs in guiôuo.
Que hum tinha completes the reference to revenue or lands that somebody possessed.
Hei is soldier, glossed tsuwamono. Hei tsukaruru begins the maxim about exhausted soldiers; the missing i in OCR Fe is restored.

runs.text: caruru toqinba, xǒ no i. voconauarezu.

lines.note: Hei tsukaruru toki(n)ba, sho no i okonawarezu: when soldiers are exhausted, the commander's authority cannot operate. The i is Japanese 威, not an explanatory label.

runs.text: Quando os ſoldados eſtão canſados o

lines.note: Xix is the citation label preceding the Portuguese translation, not OCR Aiz. The translation starts with exhausted soldiers.

runs.text: capitão não tem poder nem brio. S.

lines.note: The captain has neither power nor spirit; S marks written usage. This completes the preceding maxim rather than defining a new word.

runs.text: Hua cana com hũs papeis cortados na põta,

lines.note: A distinct hei is a ritual wand: a cane with cut paper at its tip. The repeated Fei headword was read as rei by OCR.

runs.text: conq̃ fazem certas ceremonias diante do cami.

lines.note: The wand is used for ceremonies before the kami. The scan ends cami with punctuation, not a continuation into the next entry.

runs.text: Parede de barro cuberta de taboas, ou pa-

lines.note: Another hei is a wall of earth covered with boards or straw. Parede corrects a Portuguese F/P confusion.

runs.text: lha com que cercão a caſa, ou algum chão.

lines.note: The wall encloses a house or a piece of ground; palha completes the preceding divided word.
Hei wo tsukuru / suru means constructing the wall. Feiuo restores the Japanese word already established by the headword and example.
Fazer esta cerca continues the wall-building explanation. A second example begins hei no te-.
Completes te-jin in hei no tejin awasuru, explained as enclosing a fortress with this wall. The printed j, not long s, supports the military term.
Parede completes the explanation of the fortress enclosure; no new Japanese material occurs here.

runs.text: Fei an. Tairacani yaſuxi. i, Anuon.

lines.note: Heian is peace, with tairakani yasushi and anwon as explanatory Japanese forms. The gloss paz corroborates correction of OCR reian and Iairacani.
Quietacao adds quiet or tranquility to paz, completing the heian definition.

runs.text: Eſteos de pao da parede da cerca.

lines.note: Heibashira denotes the wooden posts of the enclosing wall; esteos de pao makes the compound's hashira element explicit.
Heika, mihashi no moto, refers to the foot of the imperial steps. This is the literal courtly sense rather than merely a modern title.

runs.text: Dairi, aos degraos da qual ſe ſobe conforme a

lines.note: Dairi names the imperial palace. The steps may be ascended according to rank, with the condition completed below.
Dignidade de cada hum completes the rank-dependent access to the palace steps.
Heikai is shackles, glossed tegase and ashigase. Tegaxe corrects OCR Iegaxe; the objects bind hands and feet.
Heikai no seme wo kuwayuru means subjecting someone to torment with those restraints; Atormentar is physically divided.

runs.text: tormentar com ferros nas mãos, & nos pès.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies irons on hands and feet, supporting the paired Japanese tegase/ashigase gloss.
A homophonous heikai is closing and opening, glossed toji hiraku. Keep it distinct from the shackles entry above.
